title: Throughput benchmarking harness and methodology (wip-4)
content:
Goal:
Deliver a repeatable, low-variance harness and methodology for measuring end-to-end server throughput for the Redwood serving runtime across model variants, quantizations, and hardware profiles. This doc captures the current recommended configs, measurement rules, and known caveats (WIP).

Summary / TL;DR:
- Use a controlled two-phase run: long warmup (traffic + state warmup) then measurement window with stable RPS.
- Capture and report token/s (aggregate) + per-request latency percentiles (p50, p90, p95, p99) and tail token latency where applicable.
- Record full environment metadata (commit, model hash, quantization, image id, driver versions, GPU serials).
- Run N=5 independent trials per config; report median of medians and inter-trial variance.

Motivation / Context:
- We frequently see single-run variability driven by cold caches, CUDA/JIT warmups, dynamic batching adaptivity, and cluster background noise.
- A standardized harness reduces time spent investigating variance and gives product teams reliable baselines for rollouts and cost estimates.

Definitions:
- Throughput: tokens generated per second (tokens/s) observed at the serving layer (end-to-end).
- RPS: requests per second. For streaming models we primarily use tokens/s, for non-streaming both requests/s and tokens/s matter.
- Warmup: the period where model weights, kernels, JIT paths, and KV cache reach steady-state.
- Measurement window: the period after warmup where metrics are considered for reporting.

High-level harness components:
1) Load generator (loadgen):
   - Internal loadgen: python-based harness using asyncio and a pool of workers that send signed API requests to the runtime.
   - Requirements: support for Poisson arrivals, constant RPS, and closed-loop concurrency styles; support per-request payload templating; ability to drive streaming and chunked responses.
   - Output: per-request JSON logs with timestamps, token counts, latency start/end, and status codes.

2) Orchestration scripts:
   - Launch job that sets target RPS/concurrency, model variant, quantization flags, and GPU isolation (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES).
   - Ensures collector (prometheus pushgateway / file) is started and env metadata blob is written before warmup begins.

3) Collector + postproc:
   - Collect per-request logs, exporter metrics (gpu_util, gpu_mem, cpu, host network), kernel-level counters (if available).
   - Post-process to compute tokens/s, latency percentiles, batching stats (average batch size, max batch size), and KV cache hit rates.

Load patterns to measure:
- Constant RPS: steady stream of requests at fixed RPS; useful for stable throughput number.
- Poisson: randomizes inter-arrival times to simulate real-world variance; exposes queueing effects.
- Closed-loop concurrency: X concurrent clients; each client sends a request and waits for response before issuing next. Models adaptive batching behavior differently.
- Burst tests: short high-intensity bursts (spikes) to validate autoscale / overflow behavior and fallback policies.

Payload templates / tokens:
- Use representative prompt templates for the workload being benchmarked. Provide 3 canonical sizes per model family: short (16-32 tokens), medium (64-128 tokens), long (256-512 tokens).
- For generative throughput measurements report both input tokens and generated tokens. Standardize on generated tokens = 256 where possible for comparability.

Batching and runtime config knobs to record:
- Dynamic batching enabled/disabled, max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms.
- Max_tokens_per_request, stop_sequences, sampling params (temp, top_p) — sampling can change throughput due to sampling overhead.
- KV caching: enabled/disabled, cache size, eviction policy.
- Quantization mode: float16, int8, q4_0, q4_1, etc and the model weight artifact id.

Warmup methodology:
- Rationale: first N requests often suffer from JIT/CuDNN kernel selection, memory alloc patterns, and model cache misses. Warmup avoids measuring these transient effects.
- Warmup policy (recommended):
   1) Binary warmup: run warmup until two conditions are met: 1) at least T_min wall time elapsed (recommended 120s) AND 2) observed rolling metric (batch size, tokens/s) has stabilized (relative change < 3% over last 30s).
   2) Conservative default: fixed 5 minutes of warm traffic for GPU-backed runs with dynamic batching and large models (>10B).
   3) For quick iterations: fixed 2 minutes for small models or CPU runs.
- Warmup traffic should exercise representative token lengths and sampling settings. For KV-cache experiments, warmup must include typical prefix shapes to populate caches.

Measurement windows and repeatability:
- Use measurement windows of at least 5 minutes for steady-state metrics; 10 minutes for large variance scenarios (shared infra).
- Run 5 independent trials (full warmup + measurement) for each config. Trials should be separated by a cool-down and a full restart of the serving process to capture new-start variability.
- Report median across trials for primary metrics; include min/max and coefficient of variation (std/mean).
- If variance > 7% for tokens/s across trials, increase trials to N=9 or investigate noise source.

Metric set to capture and report (required):
- tokens_per_second (median across measurement window)
- requests_per_second (if applicable)
- latency_ms_p50, p90, p95, p99 (end-to-end request latency)
- token_latency_ms_p50,p90,p99 when streaming tokens reported separately
- avg_batch_size, batch_size_std, batch_rate (batches/sec)
- GPU_util_percent, GPU_mem_MB, CPU_util_percent
- KV_cache_hit_rate (if applicable)
- error_rate (HTTP 5xx/4xx or framework errors)
- metadata: git_commit, image_id, model_artifact_id, driver_version, cuda_version, GPU_model, run_id, hostname

Data hygiene and artifact naming:
- Each trial produces: run_id_<timestamp>_<config>.tar.gz containing: per-request JSON lines, exporter metrics (prometheus), system logs, and env metadata.json (flat k/v pairs).
- Naming convention: throughput_<model>_<quant>_<gpu>_<payload>_<rps>_<trial>.csv (or .jsonl)

Post-processing and reporting:
- Use the postproc script to parse per-request logs and compute metrics. The script should be versioned in the repo and referenced by git commit in metadata.
- Produce a single summary CSV per config with one row per trial and columns for all required metrics plus env metadata.
- For dashboards: push summary metrics to the QA prometheus namespace and generate a standardized PDF report for stakeholders.

Significance and acceptance criteria for changes:
- New runtime kernel / optimization is considered non-regressive if tokens/s >= baseline_tokens_s * 0.985 and p99 latency does not increase more than 5% for same config.
- For changes that improve latency/throughput, run full regression suite across short/medium/long payloads and at least two GPU types (A100, H100) before marking as performance-improvement.

Profiling tie-ins (when to escalate to profiler):
- If avg_batch_size deviates >20% from expectation given the same RPS: investigate scheduling, queueing, or backpressure.
- If GPU_util < 30% while latency high: suspect kernel stalls, memory thrashing, or host bottlenecks; escalate to nvprof/nsys trace.
- If p99 latency grows unbounded with increased RPS at low avg_batch_size: investigate serialization locking and critical sections.

Known pitfalls / caveats:
- Dynamic batching adaptivity: closed-loop clients change effective batch shapes. Use multiple load patterns to fully characterize behavior.
- Variance from noisy neighbors in shared infra: prefer isolated nodes or Dedicated pool for baseline numbers.
- Driver/JIT variance: small improvements in CUDA or libcudnn can change first-run timings; always record driver versions.
- Sampling randomness: stochastic decoding (temp, top_p) can change token generation time. Use deterministic sampling where possible for tight comparison.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we standardize on a single loadgen implementation (internal) or support wrk-style synthetic drivers? (TODO: vote in eng-rt sync)
- Define exact thresholds for "stabilized" metric during warmup (current guess: 3% over 30s). Need statistical validation.
- Add automated post-run anomaly detection to flag trials with unusual batch-size distributions.

Quick start checklist (for contributors):
1) Checkout serving-runtime at commit X (record hash).
2) Build docker image: make bench-image (record image id).
3) Ensure GPU node isolated: export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and stop unrelated services.
4) Start exporter and collector.
5) Kick off harness: python loadgen/run_benchmark.py --model <artifact> --quant q4_1 --rps 100 --payload medium --warmup 300 --measure 600 --outdir ./runs/<run_id>
6) Wait for run completion and upload artifacts to GCS path gs://redwood-bench/<run_id>

Appendix: example minimal loadgen config (yaml)
---
# name: baseline-medium
model: "gpt-xxx"
quant: "q4_1"
pattern: "constant_rps"
rps: 80
payload_profile: "medium"
warmup_seconds: 300
measure_seconds: 600
clients: 16
batch_timeout_ms: 25
---

Notes to reviewers:
- This file is intentionally a working doc; expect edits to warmup rules and measurement windows as we accumulate more runs.
- If you add a new metric into postproc, make sure the metadata contract (flat string keys) is updated so artifacts remain machine-readable.

-- Alex
